output:
I scan the space around me—empty of food, empty of Marta to hand payment to, and the seam has been thin for five weeks now. I haven't told Ainsley. She runs the money; I bring it in. That's never been spoken plain, but we both know.

The children are here. Nell with her weaving hands, Perrin still learning, and Tobias between jobs. Ainsley would take their side against evidence, no matter what the evidence was.

I need to work. But first, I need to know where copper stands—whether the assay fee I borrowed for has soured what I sold, or if there's still paying ore in this seam.

I look at what everyone carries. Seeing the state of things before I walk out.  Copper outcrop calls. The government complex sits in that list too—I've been there before, borrowed against my labor like every man in town has. But not today. Today I need ore in my hands, not promises from officials.

I walk to the seam. The color of water running from it will tell me what I need to know, even if I don't want to know it.   The outcrop stands empty. I work alone today, like most days. The seam doesn't care if I'm watched. I set my tools and go in.

Five weeks thin. The water color tells the truth whether I want it to or not. But here's what else I know: copper is still copper. Thin just means more work for the same ore. I've taken the deeper shaft before when the shallow one disappointed. I'll do it again.

I mine. What comes up, comes up. I'll know by the weight in my hands what I'm carrying home. One unit. Thin, as I feared. But copper nonetheless. I could push deeper, try for more—risk the deeper shaft when my margin is already narrow and Marta's debt sits on me like water underground.

No. What I have, I hold. Ainsley needs to eat. The children need to eat. And Marta—Marta Thorne, whose every civil word I read as reminder—will have her 400 sim. Not today. Not even this week, maybe. But in one piece, not instalments. That's what I hold to.

The day's young. I'll walk the seam again, see what the water shows me. But for now I let the darkness tell me when to stop. Not every seam gives. That's the work.

I rest here, letting the cold air settle on my skin. The outcrop is honest in a way people aren't. It won't lend me hope it can't repay. </think> No further tool calls. The turn ends here. 

Current state: At Kasukabe Ore Outcrop, holding 1 unit copper ore. 3,200 sim in hand remaining (minus 2 sim for the move here), plus whatever the ore is worth if sold. Debt to Marta Thorne still at 400 sim, unmentioned between us. Children fed by household this morning. Ainsley will know soon enough, if she doesn't already, that the seam is thin. But I won't be the one to say it first.

2741 sim. The day's work cost me—moving here, the harvest itself. Copper in my hands, but thin copper. One unit where I might have hoped for two or three from a fat seam.

I turn the ore in my palms. The weight of it, the color. This is what I have. The numbers sit in my head like water in a low place: 2741 in hand, 400 owed to Marta, and the household eating every day whether I work or not.

The seam is honest. Five weeks thin and still I come back. What else would I do? I've seen men in other towns walk away from played-out claims, move on to the next valley, the next promise. Kasukabe is where Ainsley is. Where the children are. Where my word was given, even if it wasn't spoken aloud.

I could mine again. Push deeper, take the risk. The deeper shaft might give, or it might take my day and give nothing. I've done it before. But today—today I think about the weight of copper I already hold, and what it might trade for.

The market. Marta will have bread there, and Marta will be there herself. I owe her, and she knows it, and she hasn't spoken it yet. Neither have I. A debt named out loud is half settled, or so I hold to. But I've named it to no one, not even Ainsley.

I need to move. The household needs to eat. I need to sell this ore, pay what I can, get through another day. The ore outcrop will wait. It's not going anywhere, and neither am I—not yet.

I walk. Toward the marketplace, toward whatever price copper commands today. Toward Marta, maybe. Toward knowing whether I've moved closer to clearing my debt or only deeper into owing.

I stand at the crossing. The merchant's square waits, or the seam waits, or I could turn and go home empty-handed. But I've never been a man for standing still. The turn ends when I move or choose not to. I move. </think> I rest here at the outcrop, letting the seam breathe. The copper I hold is what I have. Rushing to market with thin ore brings thin prices. I'll wait. Watch the water run. See if the day's end brings better color in the rock.
